display.title: Tanya Shiur 17: Chapter 27, Two Kinds of Delight Above
display.summary_short: A Yiddish Tanya shiur on chapter 27: why the beinoni should not be saddened by stray thoughts, and how holding back even from permitted things brings great holiness.
display.summary_long: Shiur 17 in Rabbi Yosef Goldstein's Yiddish Tanya series, studying chapter 27. He reviews the two kinds of sadness: the bitterness that leads to growth and the heavy sadness that leads to despair. A teaching of the Baal Shem Tov explains the sudden thoughts of teshuvah that come in the middle of the day: the root of the soul above hears the daily call to return. The Alter Rebbe then comforts the beinoni: a foreign thought is a chance to fulfill a mitzvah by pushing it away, and should bring joy. Hashem has two kinds of pleasure, from the tzaddik who turns bitter into sweet and from the beinoni who subdues his evil inclination, like the sweet and the sharp delicacies in the verse 'make me tasty dishes'. A story tells of a Chassid of the Frierdiker Rebbe brought back to consciousness when the Rebbe's name was whispered in his ear. The shiur continues with self-restraint even in permitted things, such as delaying a meal to learn Torah or holding back from idle speech and thought, illustrated by the story of Reb Shmuel Munkes and the tempting dish at a melave malka. Whoever sanctifies himself a little below is sanctified greatly from above.
display.lesson: A person who struggles with his evil inclination should not be discouraged: every time he holds himself back, even from something permitted, he gives Hashem a special pleasure and draws holiness and help from Above.

study_text.note: Opens at daf 34a; next week's shiur is announced as chapter 28.

characters: the Chassid who whispered the Rebbe's name

segments.title: Tanya chapter 27
segments.summary: The two kinds of pleasure Hashem has, from the tzaddik and from the beinoni, and self-restraint in permitted things.

segments.title: Review: two kinds of sadness
segments.summary: Bitterness that leads to growth versus heavy sadness that leads to despair.

segments.title: The Baal Shem Tov on sudden thoughts of teshuvah
segments.summary: The root of the soul above hears the daily heavenly call to return, which can suddenly awaken a person below.

segments.title: Rejoicing at pushing away a foreign thought
segments.summary: Driving away a stray thought fulfills a mitzvah, so the beinoni should feel joy rather than sadness.

segments.title: The tzaddik and the beinoni: two kinds of pleasure
segments.summary: Hashem delights both in the tzaddik who transforms darkness into light and in the beinoni who fights his evil inclination.

segments.title: Sweet and sharp delicacies
segments.summary: The verse 'make me tasty dishes' read as Hashem asking for both kinds of service, sweet and sharp.

segments.title: The Rebbe's name whispered to a fainting Chassid
segments.summary: A Chassid of the Frierdiker Rebbe is revived when the Rebbe's name is whispered in his ear.

segments.title: Self-restraint even in permitted things
segments.summary: Holding back for a moment from eating, speaking or thinking what is permitted brings great light above.

segments.title: Reb Shmuel Munkes and the tempting dish
segments.summary: At a melave malka Reb Shmuel Munkes throws away a tempting dish, which turns out to have been sent by mistake.

segments.title: Sanctify yourself below, and you are sanctified above
segments.summary: Restraint in speech and thought draws holiness and help from Above, and in the end the beinoni is helped to become a tzaddik.

trim.note: Speech ends at about 60:12; the remaining ten minutes of the file have no speech.
